articleHeadline: Cochrane Map Reveals Major Gaps in Dengue Research
articleSummary: Dengue prevention research mapped by Cochrane reveals abundant studies but few are synthesized into actionable, high-quality systematic reviews. The global map, published in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews on 2026-08-24, identifies dengue spread by Aedes aegypti with Brazil reporting among the highest case numbers and disproportionate impact on marginalized communities. While research spans community education, vector control, vaccines, and environmental interventions, critical gaps remain in systematic reviews—especially for adult vector and aquatic-stage interventions, implementation, and behavioural outcomes. Of note, the adult dengue vaccine evidence mainly lacks real-world implementation data. Among 47 randomized trials and 140 non-randomized studies for community education, evidence on its impact on transmission is inconclusive. The EGM prioritizes four areas: environmental interventions, community education, aquatic-stage and adult-vector interventions. The authors urge updated vector-control reviews, better synthesis of implementation/behavioural data, and evaluation of adverse effects beyond vaccines; emphasize epidemiological outcomes over entomological surrogates.

Farmers growing their own material are urged to select healthy, vigorous plants. Senave requests permanent field surveillance and immediate reporting of suspicious symptoms by technicians, with active participation in inspections.

articleSummary: Delhi-NCR is reporting rising H1N1 (swine flu) illnesses alongside flu-like symptoms, prompting health guidance. Not everyone with H1N1 develops severe illness; risk is higher for older adults, young children, pregnant women, and people with certain conditions. Fever alone does not diagnose H1N1, since dengue, seasonal influenza, and COVID-19 can cause similar symptoms. articleHeadline: How To Avoid Contracting H1N1 In A Corporate Office: Doctors Share Essential Prevention Tips
articleSummary: H1N1 influenza presents a rapid transmission risk in enclosed corporate offices, where air-conditioning, open-plan seating, and shared meeting rooms facilitate airborne and surface spread. Lab studies show H1N1 persistence on non-porous surfaces for 24–48 hours and lingering aerosols (<5 μm) in unventilated spaces, underscoring the need for proper ventilation and filtration. Clinicians advocate a layered approach: 1) annual vaccination; 2) reinforced desk-surface hygiene with alcohol-based sanitizers (60%+) to curb fomite transmission; 3) optimized indoor airflow and symptom isolation, with symptomatic individuals using N95 masks or remote work. A practical workstation checklist includes sanitizing high-touch gear, avoiding desk dining, staying home when unwell, and maintaining mucosal hydration. Indian hospital clinicians emphasize these measures to minimize H1N1 spread in workplaces.

articleSummary: Shenzhen, Guangdong Province, China reports a case of Angiostrongylus cantonensis (rat lungworm) infection causing eosinophilic meningitis in a 1-year-old girl who developed high fever and severe encephalitis after playing in a community. The culprit snail is the African giant snail (Achatina fulica), palm-sized, an invasive species native to East Africa listed by IUCN among the world’s 100 worst invasive species; in southern China it can live 5–6 years, reproduce up to four times yearly, and lay over 6,000 eggs in a lifetime. The snail is an intermediate host for Angiostrongylus cantonensis and can carry other pathogens. Humans may acquire infection by eating raw or undercooked snail meat containing third-stage larvae, or consuming vegetables or water contaminated with larvae, leading to meningitis or brain inflammation. Prevention emphasizes avoiding contact with the snail and secretions; wash exposed skin, disinfect wounds, monitor for fever or headache, and seek care if symptoms appear; notify management if large snail gatherings are found.

articleSummary: 16,250 Ervebo doses landed in Kinshasa on Aug 22 for the Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak in the DRC, which has 5,515 confirmed cases and 2,642 deaths (case fatality ~48%).
